prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Othello (Reversi) on an 8x8 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: np.ndarray, opponent: np.ndarray) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move when `policy` is called. - `you` and `opponent` are 8x8 numpy arrays containing only 0/1 integers. - `you[r][c] == 1` means your disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - `opponent[r][c] == 1` means the opponent disc is at row `r`, col `c`. - An empty cell means `you[r][c] == 0` and `opponent[r][c] == 0`. - Positions are valid: never `you[r][c] == opponent[r][c] == 1`. - Move coordinates use algebraic notation: columns `a..h` map to `c = 0..7`, rows `1..8` map to `r = 0..7`. For example, `a4` maps to you[3][0] - The game ends when neither player has a legal move (or the board is full). - Objective: finish with more discs than the opponent; ties are draws. # Action / Return Format - Return a move string like `"d3"` (file letter `a..h` + rank `1..8`). - A legal move must place a disc on an empty cell that flips at least one opponent disc in any direction. - Flips occur along any of the 8 directions where the new disc brackets a contiguous line of opponent discs ending in your disc. - If you have no legal moves, return `"pass"`. You may not return `"pass"` if you have legal moves. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...

For endgame with 12-13 empties, I can go exact using iterative deepening negamax alpha-beta, returning the best move from the last fully completed depth if time runs out, with an exact disc-difference eval once depth reaches remaining empties. I'll implement this with a transposition table keyed on the board state, storing depth, value, flag, and best move, using TT-move-first ordering followed by static ordering favoring corners.

For move ordering among children, I'll keep it cheap by sorting on positional weight of the square initially, then add opponent-mobility-based ordering at deeper nodes (depth >= 3) since fewer opponent replies tends to be stronger, avoiding redundant move generation costs where possible.

For evaluation, I'm defining a function that scores from the mover's perspective by combining move-count differentials with a positional weight table, using bit_count-based popcounting for speed and falling back gracefully on older Python versions. I want to avoid iterating bit-by-bit over 64 squares for the positional score, so I'm thinking of precomputing per-byte-row weight tables to speed that lookup up.

I'm also planning stability estimation by anchoring at corners and extending along edges while the color stays consistent, treating fully-occupied edges as automatically stable, and I want to penalize frontier discs — those touching empty squares — as a proxy for weak positions.

I'm now weighting these features by game phase: mobility, corner control, edge stability, and frontier count matter most early-to-mid game, while raw disc count and stability dominate as the board fills up. I'll tune the weights roughly rather than perfectly, since most opponents in the arena are likely simple heuristic or random players rather than deep searchers.

I'm setting up the standard positional weight table that rewards corners heavily and penalizes X-squares adjacent to empty corners, but that penalty should disappear once the neighboring corner is actually captured.

I'm actually thinking a proper stable-disc calculation would capture corner value better than static weights, and considering implementing it efficiently with bitboards by checking full lines and adjacency to already-stable discs.

Actually, stability could be computed iteratively: a disc is stable if along each of the 4 axes, either the line is full, or a neighbor already deemed stable exists in that direction. Iterating this a few times to fixpoint costs extra bit ops per eval, roughly doubling per-position cost, so I'll only bother computing stability when it's actually needed rather than at every node.
